dedupe_keys.name: vegetation clearance distances to prevent wildland fire damage to telecommunication and power towers and poles usfs 2015

description: This proceedings paper from the Large Wildland Fires Conference (Missoula, May 2014) reports preliminary findings from two independent studies of how far vegetation must be cleared to stop wildland fire from damaging towers and poles that carry telecommunication and power lines. It finds that steel towers resist fire damage best but fail catastrophically when they fail, while wood poles and towers do not fail catastrophically; minimum clearances are 1 to 21 m for steel towers in surface and crown fires, 1 to 33 m for wood poles in low to moderate surface fires, and 20 to 33 m for wood poles and towers in crown fires in tall brush and canopy. Ignition risk of wood poles depends on the age and condition of the surface, and clearance around telecommunication towers depends on exposed cables, guy wires and nearby materials. Producer: Butler, Webb, Hogge and Wallace, Rocky Mountain Research Station, published in Proceedings RMRS-P-73, pages 35 to 40, in 2015 (informally refereed). Coverage: United States, based on the two studies. Access: a free PDF on the Treesearch site. Licence and cost: no licence stated; free. Caveats: the authors call their analysis and conclusions preliminary, and clearances are ranges, not a validated model. Simulation uses: the clearance ranges give fragility and hazard exposure inputs for wildfire risk assessment of telecom and power supports. Related records: none found for this specific topic.
